data.title: UBS Sends Stark Warning to Nike Stock Investors
data.description:
Nike is facing another warning from Wall Street, with UBS cutting its price target to $42 from $48 as deteriorating sales trends raise the risk of weaker earnings and another reset to fiscal 2027 expectations.

UBS analyst Jay Sole maintained a Neutral rating but said the firm's recent channel checks show Nike's global sales growth trend has worsened over the past three months.

That comes with shares already under heavy pressure.

Nike recently traded around $35.78, just above its 52-week low of $35.76, and the stock has fallen roughly 49% over the past year.

UBS expects Nike to miss fiscal first-quarter 2027 earnings estimates by about 5 cents per share.

More importantly, the firm expects management to provide an implied fiscal second-quarter EPS outlook of roughly 31 cents to 43 cents, well below the Street's current 53-cent estimate.

UBS also sees a risk that Nike uses the upcoming earnings report to lower fiscal 2027 expectations ahead of its November investor day.

The firm believes investors remain too optimistic about the magnitude of potential earnings revisions.

According to UBS, the next report could push Wall Street EPS estimates lower and further weaken sentiment.

Options markets appear prepared for significant volatility, pricing in an approximately 8% move around the event compared with Nike's historical average move of about 6.7%.

Investors Takeaway

The key risk is that the stock's nearly 50% decline has not yet fully captured the deterioration in earnings.

That matters because low share prices alone do not create a valuation floor if profit estimates continue moving lower.

UBS is effectively arguing that Nike could face another leg of estimate cuts before the turnaround becomes visible.

Investors should watch global sales trends, gross margins, fiscal 2027 guidance and management's November investor-day strategy.

The bull case is that expectations have already fallen dramatically, creating room for upside if sales stabilize.

The bearish case is that Nike's earnings base keeps shrinking faster than the stock's valuation adjusts.

With Morgan Stanley, BMO and UBS all highlighting downside risks, the next earnings report could become an important test of whether Nike's turnaround is merely slow or still deteriorating.

Press Release – Corporate News

Luxembourg, 18 September 2026

CPI Property Group – Sale of 27 Savile Row

CPI Property Group (“CPIPG” or the “Group”) has completed the sale of our property at 27 Savile Row in London. The Group acquired 27 Savile Row in 2021 and subsequently secured planning permissions for a new office scheme. In response to strong investor interest, the Group decided to sell the property rather than undertake the development ourselves. The gross transaction price was about GBP 105 million.

CPIPG purchased 27 Savile Row from the Metropolitan Police through a public tender process. The building previously served as the central police station for London’s West End. From the outset, the Group identified the site’s significant redevelopment potential. Savile Row is one of the most prestigious addresses in London’s Mayfair district, located just moments from Bond Street, Regent Street and other prime destinations in the West End. The area benefits from a limited supply of new office developments and consistently strong demand for best-in-class office space.

In recent years, CPIPG and our UK development partner, Henigman, worked with the London-based architectural practice PLP Architecture to develop The Row, a new office project for the site. The approved scheme includes a new office building with approximately 4,350 m² of gross floor area, together with a restaurant and outdoor terraces. The project targets BREEAM Outstanding and WELL Platinum certifications, a 5-star NABERS rating and an EPC A energy rating. It also retains approximately 95% of the existing stone façade, reflecting the project’s commitment to sustainable redevelopment.

“CPIPG acquired 27 Savile Row because we saw the potential to create an exceptional new office scheme. By securing the necessary planning permissions, we created substantial value which has now been realized, consistent with our strategy to sell non-yielding development assets.” said Michal Felcman, Deputy COO of CPIPG.

Scott Lister of Michael Elliott LLP and Scott Curtis of CMS Cameron McKenna Nabarro Olswang LLP acted on behalf of CPIPG.

“This sale reflects the high quality of the property, good transaction structuring, and excellent timing. 27 Savile Row attracted strong market interest, and CPIPG was able to convert that interest into a transaction that meets the Group’s strategic objectives,” said Květa Vojtová, Group Head of M&A and Transactional Legal at CPIPG.

data.title: French bond spread at highest since 2012 as default insurance spikes
data.description:
By Yoruk Bahceli and Amanda Cooper

Investor concerns over France's stretched finances ahead of next year's elections drove the risk premium on French government bonds to its highest level since the euro zone debt crisis on Friday, while the cost of insuring the country's debt also rose sharply.

The spread on French 10-year government bonds over Germany's rose as high as 104 basis points, (DE10FR10=RR) exceeding a whole percentage point for the first time since 2012, as investors demand higher compensation for the risk of holding the debt.

Yields on benchmark 10-year French bonds (FR10YT=RR) rose 10 bps to 4.456%. French yields have risen faster than those of any other developed economy in a selloff driven by higher energy prices that has rattled global government debt markets in recent weeks.

France is proving particularly vulnerable in the bond selloff as it faces a challenging budget and struggles to get its fiscal position in order ahead of a presidential election next year that could make that task even harder.

France's government plans to include a €54 billion ($62 billion) savings drive in its 2027 budget to stop the ​fiscal deficit spiralling out of control, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Thursday, as protests over high ‌fuel prices swell.

It will already miss this year's budget deficit target as the economy will grow less than previously expected this year.

"Investors in general they are not too confident in stepping (in) and buying, and I think that's what is driving this ongoing grind wider in spreads," said Evelyne Gomez-Liechti, multi-asset strategist at Mizuho in London, adding that the bank was seeing little flow in French debt.

"Everyone is sidelined and not willing to buy here just in case it keeps grinding wider and wider."

French 5-year credit default swaps, a form of protection against the risk of default, hit 41.5 bps , the highest level since the "Liberation Day" turmoil unleashed by U.S. President Donald Trump's blanket tariffs in April last year.

They were up nearly 3 bps since Thursday's close in their biggest one-day increase since mid-March, when the Iran war whipped up market volatility.

French bank stocks were also hit, with BNP Paribas down 3.6%, while Credit Agricole and Societe Generale were each down 2.5%.

France's blue-chip CAC index was down 1.5%, slightly underperforming other regional indices.

($1 = 0.8724 euros)

data.title: Wall St slips as higher Treasury yields weigh on sentiment
data.description:
Key points:
  • Indexes: Dow down 0.36%, S&P 500 down 0.10%, Nasdaq down 0.02%
  • Buffett steps down as Berkshire chair
  • Xenon Pharmaceuticals slides after trial setback

By Niket Nishant and Tharuniyaa Lakshmi

Wall Street's main indexes fell on Friday in the final stretch of a turbulent week, as investors digested shifting oil prices, higher Treasury yields and a Federal Reserve rate hike.

The quarterly expiration of derivatives contracts tied to stocks, index options and futures, known as "triple witching," also threatened to exacerbate volatility.

Nine of the 11 major S&P 500 sector indexes were lower, and the materials index led losses with a 1.3% decline.

The interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve and Chair Kevin Warsh's commentary on the future trajectory of borrowing costs has kept investors busy this week.

"We expect more volatility ahead as markets digest the move," said Motley Fool Asset Management's Chief Investment Strategist Bill Mann.

"In this environment, staying invested in the highest-quality companies gives investors the best chance to weather the turbulence and capitalize on the opportunities it creates."

Investors also reassessed the outlook for AI demand this week after top industry executives urged a slowdown in the development of the technology. There is little clarity yet on what such a slowdown would look like.

The race for AI supremacy is set to hang over next week's meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.

With the earnings season still a month away, commentary from top industry executives at a string of conferences this week gave markets an early read on corporate health and helped shape sentiment.

"The recent strength of S&P 500 earnings growth has raised investor concerns that the market is in an 'earnings bubble'," wrote Ben Snider, chief US equity strategist at Goldman Sachs.

"While there are indeed factors contributing to 'over-earning' today, our base case is for S&P 500 earnings growth to decelerate, not collapse, in coming years."

At 11:29 a.m. ET, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 187.03 points, or 0.36%, to 51,591.86, the S&P 500 lost 7.67 points, or 0.10%, to 7,630.23 and the Nasdaq Composite shed 5.84 points, or 0.02%, to 26,412.53.

Crude prices were volatile on Friday, as markets weighed supply concerns following fresh strikes between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.

The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury rose 5.3 bps to 5%.

Meanwhile, Xenon Pharmaceuticals tumbled over 29% after it temporarily paused ​enrolment in tests for its experimental drug for ‌major and bipolar depression following reports of side effects.

Berkshire Hathaway said Warren Buffett, its former CEO and one of the world's most revered investors, will step down as chairman and become chairman emeritus, effective immediately. Class B shares of the company were 0.3% lower.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 1.3%, helped by Nvidia and Intel .

Crypto stocks also rose, with Coinbase , Strategy and Robinhood gaining 10%, 12% and 8%, respectively. A sharp gain in bitcoin took it past $80,000.

Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 2.44-to-1 ratio on the NYSE and by a 1.84-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq.

The S&P 500 posted 5 new 52-week highs and 27 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 30 new highs and 104 new lows.

data.title: Stocks Bend, but Don't Break, in Head-Spinning September. More Tests Are Coming. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Martin Baccardax

U.S. stocks enter the final throes of September pretty much on pace with the kind of declines expected over the market's historically weakest month, having fought through issues that could have pushed them firmly lower into the close of the third quarter.

A massive surge in Treasury bond yields, which lifted 10-year notes to the highest since 2007, paired with a worrying summer rally in global crude prices that has oil trading firmly north of $100 a barrel, leaned heavily on stocks but didn't tip them over.

A Federal Reserve interest-rate hike, coupled with hawkish language and quickening inflation forecasts, also came and went, with stocks posting their strongest gains in six weeks and an index of the Magnificent Seven tech giants coming within half a point of the all-time high it reached in late May.

Tech stocks, in fact, have largely weathered a series of "end of days" headlines from the AI space, with an index of semiconductor stocks falling around 3.3% over the past month and those in the information technology edging just 1.2% lower despite the torrent of stories tied to apocalyptic AI risks.

Yet through all that, the S&P 500 is down around 0.8% for the month, largely in line with the average September decline since the 1950s, with the Nasdaq Composite holding on to its end of August levels.

The resilience is important heading into a barren three-week stretch for markets, followed by the third quarter earnings season with an update from JPMorgan on Oct. 13, and the potentially game-changing midterm elections on Nov. 3.

"The stock market has held up very well so far in September, but remains on eggshells thanks to rising oil prices and bond yields," said Rick Gardner, chief investment officer at RGA Investments in Raleigh, N.C.

"But we're not out of the woods when it comes to the volatility that typically arises during September and October," he added.

Earnings are likely to provide near-term support, however, with analysts expecting collective S&P 500 profits for the three months ending in September to surge 30% from last year to around $768.8 billion.

That would put the index on pace for a full year gain of around 35%, the strongest since 2021, thanks largely to the tech and AI spending that has powered markets higher since the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022.

But can it lean on the faster inflation metrics, and the leg higher analysts are expecting in Treasury yields, into the final months of the year?

Brent crude, the global pricing benchmark for oil, has surged nearly 50% over the past 21/2 months, pushing domestic gas prices nearly 40% higher on the year and taking diesel fuel costs to the highest on record at $6.45 a gallon.

Those elements will wreak havoc on inflation readings over the coming months, with Jeffrey Gundlach, founder of DoubleLine Capital, suggesting CPI readings will soon spike north of 4%.

"The psychology is that inflation is now trending higher," he told CNBC earlier this week, citing inventory buildups in GDP readings and Costco's decision to double the price of its Kirkland branded motor oil. "But I worry that the problem isn't being respected."

Bond markets are clearly concerned, with 10-year yields trending close to the 5% mark on Friday, having pulled back to as low as 4.935% during Thursday's solid equity rally. An increasing number of Wall Street analysts are forecasting higher levels over the coming months.

John Davies, U.S. rate strategist at Standard Chartered, sees 10-year yields hitting 5.5% over the next 12 months, and testing 5.1% by the end of the year, "until the market is more confident that inflation will return to target."

"AI-related investment and issuance, U.S. fiscal concerns, and Japanese repatriation risks remain either active or potential challenges" to the market, he added, "even if the impact of oil prices on yields eventually fades."

Higher rates for longer, alongside a likely change in the composition of the House of Representatives, where Democrats hold a solid lead in polling into the November vote, will pose significant challenges for stocks into the close of the year.

Not everyone agrees, however.

"Equity and bond investors are arguably overreacting" to both the Fed's recent hawkishness and the assumption of faster inflation reading blunting broader markets, said Fundstrat's Tom Lee.

"That 'max hawkish' stance creates a bullish setup for equities," he added, citing the likelihood of softer jobs data, muted inflation readings under a new PCE measuring format, and the lack of concern seen in broader VIX volatility readings, which remain pinned near the lowest levels of the year.

"We think there is a positive setup into month end, and the up move could be very sharply positive," Lee said.

Autumn is approaching, the leaves are about to change and the weather will soon be colder.

Stocks will change, too. But just how much remains to be seen.

Write to Martin Baccardax at martin.baccardax@barrons.com

data.title: Alphabet stock jumps as Wall Street raises targets and search rebounds
data.description:
Wall Street is offering another vote of confidence in Alphabet Inc. (GOOGL, Financials), the parent firm of Google, which is a key player in advertising, cloud computing and artificial intelligence.

Shares climbed in premarket trade after Evercore ISI analyst Mark Mahaney boosted his price objective to $450 from $420, citing new data showing Google's search position has rebounded.

In its most recent poll, Evercore revealed that 78% of respondents said they used Google as their preferred search engine in August. That's up from a low of 70% in 2024 and early 2025.

This change significant because AI-powered search has been one of the major risks that investors have dreaded. Instead, Mahaney said Google's search leadership has improved over the last year and he boosted his expectations for Google's search revenue through 2028.

Now, his sales and operating income estimates for 2028 are 4% to 5% above the Wall Street consensus.

Alphabet also benefited from a Sept. 16 court verdict that fell short of requiring Google to divest its ad-tech division. The corporation has been ordered to adjust its advertising tactics and to allow monitoring for six years.

Tigress Financial also increased its price target to $485 from $415.

The next question is whether increased search use and AI investment can convert into sustainable earnings growth as Alphabet faces stricter scrutiny and higher spending.

data.title: Jungle Camps India appoints Bharat Mandhyan as Lodge Manager at Kanha Jungle Camp
data.description:
Jungle Camps India (JCI) has appointed Bharat Mandhyan as Lodge Manager at Kanha Jungle Camp, bringing three decades of wildlife tourism experience across Kanha, Bandhavgarh and Pench. His experience spans guest services, lodge operations, team management and wildlife experiences.

In his new role, Bharat will oversee the day-to-day functioning of the property, drawing on his experience across guest services, food and beverage, housekeeping, hiring and training, budgeting, inventory and marketing.

Bharat began his career as a naturalist, leading safaris, nature walks and birding excursions, while conducting wildlife lectures and working with forest authorities, drivers and guides on safari operations. He has also contributed to conservation and community initiatives in Bandhavgarh, including socio-economic development programmes, census activities and the development of eco-development plans in coordination with the Forest Department.

Gajendra Singh Rathore, Chairperson & Managing Director, Jungle Camps India, said, “Bharat brings together something that is particularly valuable in wildlife hospitality, a deep understanding of the forest alongside three decades of experience managing lodges and teams. His long association with Kanha and experience across Central India will add significant value to the team at Kanha Jungle Camp.”
